sources.news_title: Genre-defying poet and writer Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature
sources.text:
Genre-defying poet and writer Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature
See more of our coverage in your search results.
STOCKHOLM, Oct 8 (Reuters) – Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson, whose work often blends verse, prose, dialogue and translation in a genre-defying mix, won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday for what the Swedish Academy called her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”
“Crazy, I think they’re all crazy,” Carson told Icelandic broadcaster RUV when asked how she was feeling after learning she had won while on the Arctic island. “I’ll get a sticker on the front of my book.”
Carson, 76, who was born in Toronto and has a home in Iceland, had been taken by surprise when called with the news, said Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Academy, which awards the prize worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).
“All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind,” Carlberg told a press conference in Stockholm after the announcement.
She is widely known for her translations of classical Greek literature, which heavily influences her work that ranges from opera libretti to literary criticism and verse novels such as “Autobiography of Red” from 1998.
“Genre is something for booksellers. It’s something you do in order to appeal to an audience and make them buy books. And on what shelf do you put Anne Carson’s books? It’s on a shelf of her own,” said Swedish novelist Steve Sem-Sandberg, who is a member of the award committee. “That’s what I like about her.”
‘New forms of contemporary literature’
In its citation, the Swedish Academy said it was recognizing Carson “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” the Academy said.
“She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work. Her translations from Classical Greek may be regarded as independent works in their own right.”
Her style is exemplified in “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy” from 2019, a performance piece which mixes the stories of Helen of Troy in Euripides’ play “Helen” with Marilyn Monroe.
Life without Proust
Often heralded as her greatest work, “Autobiography of Red” demonstrates Carson’s ability to “actualize the classical literary tradition,” the Academy said. In the book, she re-examines age-old questions such as “What happens when you love someone who will ultimately destroy you?”
Tapping into more modern inspirations, Carson reflected on the character of Albertine, one of the narrator Marcel’s love interests in Marcel Proust’s “In Search of Lost Time,” in her own book “The Albertine Workout.”
Carson had spent seven years reading Proust’s masterpiece and said in an interview with Canada’s CBC Radio One in 2016 that she suffered withdrawal symptoms after finishing, leading her to write “The Albertine Workout” as a way to prolong the experience.
“You think life goes on after Proust, but it seems so gray,” she said.
Boxing lessons to fight Parkinson’s
Carson started taking boxing lessons when she was already in her 70s because of a Parkinson’s disease diagnosis. The sport is recommended as a therapy because it helps with paying attention to hand-eye coordination and the sequencing of actions.
She reflected on the disease’s impact on her handwriting in an interview at the Louisiana Literary Festival in Denmark in 2024: “I scrub out whole paragraphs in shame … the shame of bad handwriting.”

Thanks for signing up!
Carson, who has taught classics at universities in Canada and the United States, has said that she considers herself a visual artist as much as a literary one.
“I think of making a poem as making an object. I have always thought of them more as drawings than as texts, but drawings that are also physically enterable through the fact of language,” she said in the CBC interview.
Poetry, she says, may be more attuned to the fast modern-day life than long-form writing.
“I think it’s probably more useful than prose right now because it’s faster and everybody is in a hurry so basically it’s good because it is brief,” she told the Icelandic broadcaster on Thursday.
When asked by the Nobel Committee about her own sources of inspiration, however, she listed ancient Greek poet Homer, author of “The Odyssey” epic.
As to how the classical stories she has reinterpreted in her work might be relevant to modern audiences, she said: “I don’t think I’m interested in relevance.”
‘At home’ in Iceland and NYC
Carson and her husband, artist Robert Currie, first came to Iceland after the 2008 banking collapse and gradually spent more time there. “We got to know people and we liked the people,” Carson told Iceland Review in 2023.
She has held citizenship of Iceland since 2022.
Currie told the magazine Iceland was one of only two places that immediately felt like home to him, the other being New York City in the 1970s.
Literature was the fourth of this year’s Nobel prizes to be announced this week, following medicine, physics and chemistry. The peace prize winner will be announced in Oslo on Friday.
Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes have been awarded since 1901.
Carson, who had been among the favorites this year, takes a place beside luminaries such as Alexander Solzhenitsyn, Alice Munro and Ernest Hemingway as a recipient of the award. Last year’s prize was won by Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai.
($1 = 10.0190 Swedish crowns)

sources.news_title: Who is Anne Carson? Meet the Nobel Prize in Literature winner
How to Read All of Anne Carson’s Books in Order
sources.text:
Carson’s very first book focuses on the “paradoxical nature of romantic love,” focusing on love in ancient Greek literature in philosophy.
Her first collection of poetry, Short Talks (reissued in 2015), is a collection of prose poems. Like “Short Talk on Walking Backwards,” as published in the Yale Review: “My mother forbad us to walk backwards. That is how the dead walk, she would say. Where did she get this idea? Perhaps from a bad translation. The dead, after all, do not walk backwards but they do walk behind us. They have no lungs and cannot call out but would love for us to turn around. They are victims of love, many of them.”
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
Plainwater, Carson’s third book, is a collection of poetry and essays. Per the publisher, “these pieces stretch the boundaries of language and literary form, while juxtaposing classical and modern traditions.”
Carson weaves “contemporary and ancient poetic strands” in Glass, Irony and God. The anchor of the collection is “The Glass Essay,” a long poem that meditates on Emily Brontë and a painful romantic breakup.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
Carson’s first novel, Autobiography of Red, is written in verse, reimagining Geryoneis by Stesichorus. She later published a sequel, Red Doc>, in 2013.
In this lecture, Carson explores the idea of poetic economy, focusing on ancient Greek lyric poet Simonides of Keos and Holocaust survivor Paul Celan.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
Men in the Off Hours is another collection of poetry and pose from Carson. In the book, she writes about Oedipus, Emily Dickinson, Audubon, and more literary figures, along with personal topics like the death of her mother.
One of Carson’s first translations of Greek tragedies is that of Electra, which tells the story of the murders of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
Winner of the Los Angeles Times Book Prize in 2001, The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos, reflects on John Keats’s ideas in 29 “tangos” of narrative verse.
If Not, Winter is Carson’s translation of the work of Sappho, presented together with the original Greek.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
Simone Weil describes “decreation” as “undoing the creature in us,” and undoing the self. Carson explores this idea in Decreation, a collection of poetry in a multitude of forms, including opera libretto, screenplay, poem, oratorio, essay, shot list, and rapture.
Four of Euripides’ tragedies are translated by Carson in Grief Lessons, along with two framing essays she authored including “Tragedy: A Curious Art Form” and “Why I Wrote Two Plays About Phaidra.”
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
In An Oresteia, Carson combines three different versions of the Atreus tragedy: Aiskhylos’s Agamemnon, Sophocles’s Elektra, and Euripides’s Orestes. 
Nox, a poetry collection, centers on the loss Carson’s brother, with poems alongside old letters, family photos, collages, and sketches on pages.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
Carson’s translation of Sophocles’s Antigone features a preface, “Dear Antigone.”
The follow-up to Autobiography of Red picks up where that novel left of with the story of Geryon and Herakles.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
Nay Rather is two works by Carson: “Variations on the Right to Remain Silent,” an essay on the stakes of translation, and “By Chance the Cycladic People,” a poem about Cycladic culture.
Iphigenia among the Taurians is another translation of a play by Euripides.
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
The Albertine Workout is just fifty-nine paragraphs (plus appendices) of Carson writing about Albertine, the principal love interest of Marcel in Proust’s Á la recherche du temps perdu. 
Carson translated Antigone for a production directed by Ivo van Hove in 2015.
Emily Burack (she/her) is the Deputy Digital Editor for Town & Country, where she covers entertainment, celebrities, the royals, and a wide range of other topics. Before joining T&C, she was the deputy managing editor at Hey Alma, a Jewish culture site. Follow her @emburack on Instagram, Twitter, and other social media platforms.

sources.news_title: Anne Carson's Nobel Literature Prize 'A Proud Moment For Canada', Says PM
sources.text:
Canadian poet Anne Carson winning the Nobel prize for literature is a “proud moment” for the country, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday.
The 76-year-old’s works feature “wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own,” Carney said on X.
“She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” he said, calling the award “an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada.”
A renowned classicist, Carson has taught at several prestigious Canadian and American universities, including McGill in Montreal. She joined McGill’s Department of Classics in 1988 and left the university in 2002.
“This is a wonderfully deserved honour for Anne Carson, whose work has captivated readers around the world by bringing ancient voices into conversation with the present,” Lisa Shapiro, McGill’s dean of arts, was quoted as saying by The McGill Reporter.
“Her extraordinary talent, originality and intellectual depth have had a profound influence on contemporary literature. We are proud that McGill was her academic home for many years and delighted to see her remarkable contributions recognized on the world stage.”
Outside the university in Montreal, Vicky Huang, a 24-year-old political science student, expressed pride.
“My friends and I love ‘Eros the Bittersweet,’ so this is such exciting news,” she told AFP.
“Yeah, I mean, the fact that she’s a Canadian woman working in high literature makes all of us really proud.”

“Bold, Inventive” Professor Wins Nobel Prize in Literature
sources.text:
Pontus Lundahl/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images/Sweden OUT
Anne Carson, a poet and essayist who has taught at some of the most selective universities in the United States and Canada, won the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature Thursday. In announcing the award, the Swedish Academy cited her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
Carson’s extensive body of work reflects a range of themes and influences, including classical Greek and Roman literature, Virginia Woolf, and her own experiences. According to the Associated Press, “Autobiography of Red,” which reimagined the myth of Hercules and the monster Geryon as a love story, has sold nearly 100,000 copies in the United States alone since it debuted in 1998. Born in Toronto in 1950, she has also written translations of numerous class Greek poems and plays, including Sophocles’s Electra and Antigone and Euripides’s Bakkhai.
“Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel literature committee, told the AP.
Carson earned a doctorate in classics from the University of Toronto in 1981 and taught literature and writing at University of Calgary, McGill University, the University of Michigan, New York University and Princeton University.
“The NYU Creative Writing Program was incredibly fortunate to have had the singularly brilliant and visionary writer Anne Carson on faculty for 13 years as Distinguished Writer in Residence,” Deborah Landau, director of NYU’s creative writing program, wrote in a news release congratulating Carson. She recalled how Carson and her romantic partner and collaborator, Robert Currie, “famously taught a graduate workshop called ‘Egocircus,’ which allowed our M.F.A .students to collaborate with her on a range of artistic projects.”
When Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, reached Carson by phone Thursday, “All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind,” Carlberg told reporters. Carson, who lives in Iceland with Currie, told a local news outlet that the conversation was “rather halting.”
“I think they’re all crazy,” she said. “They have the usual questions, and I have no answers.”

sources.news_title: Canadian poet and classicist Anne Carson wins ‘crazy’ Nobel
sources.text:
Asked by RUV on a blustery roadside if she thought the Nobel would change her readership, Carson, holding tightly to her cap so it wouldn’t blow away, replied: “I’ll get a sticker on the front of my books.”
Carson had at first ignored the Academy’s repeated phone calls.
“There were all these phone calls which I kept turning off because ... I just always turn off the phone when it rings,” she said.
Her husband convinced her to call back, she told the Nobel Foundation.
A professor of classics with a background in dead languages, literature, anthropology and history, she was described by the New York Times in 2001 as “one of the great pasticheurs”.
Her unique contemporary poetry earned her several key literary prizes in the 1990s, including the 1996 Lannan Award and the 1997 Pushcart Prize.
A year later, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse – loosely based on the Greek myth of the monster Geryon and Herakles but transformed into a modern tale of a gay love triangle – received widespread praise.
‘Author for our time’ 
The Academy singled out her 2010 poem Nox, printed on one continuous sheet of paper in homage to her brother who died in 2000, as “an unforgettable work”.
“Palpable here is a deep sense of loss that works its way up from below. The result is a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother.”
It also highlighted her translations from Classical Greek, which “may be regarded as independent works in their own right”.
Academy member Steve Sem-Samberg told the Nobel Foundation Carson was “an author for our time”, connecting the contemporary with antiquity.
“She uses the myths, the characters, the stories, the fables from that time to put them into a modern context. And the mixture between those two gives an enormous energy to her writing,” he said.
“When you’re inside her work, you immediately recognise her voice and her themes. Nobody writes like her,” he told AFP.
In her own interview with the Nobel Foundation, Carson described her writing as “inadvertant”, coming about while “always trying to do something else”.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the win “an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada”.
Women under-represented 
In the London Review of Books in 2024, Carson said Parkinson’s had “disintegrated” her handwriting, a “particularly mortifying” symptom.
“I used to take pleasure in writing in notebooks, shelves of them, day after day, year after year. Now the upright strokes bend or break or go in all directions, vowels shrink to blobs, slant loses its smooth smart angle, it all looks embarrassing.”
Carson had been mentioned as a possible Nobel laureate for years, though some experts said the Academy was unlikely to honour another Canadian so soon after the 2013 prize to short story author Alice Munro.
Many literary critics had expected the award to go to a woman this year, given the frequent criticism directed at the Academy over the over-representation of Western white men among its picks.
There have been just 19 women laureates out of 122 since the Nobel literature prize was first awarded in 1901.
A 2018 sex assault scandal left the Academy in tatters and more than half of its 18 members were replaced.
Since then, every other literature laureate has been a woman.
Last year, the award went to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose works explore themes of postmodern dystopia.
The Nobel Prize comes with a diploma, a gold medal and US$1.2 million ($2.1m).
- AFP

sources.news_title: Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature for her genre-bending writing
sources.text:
Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature for her genre-bending writing
Canadian poet Anne Carson was recognized for playful, ironic works that interweave the classical and the contemporary
Saskia Grisaru • October 8, 2026
An artist’s rendering of the Canadian writer Anne Carson, who has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature [Credit: Niklas Elmehend | © Nobel Prize Outreach]
At the same hour that she was being awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm, the Canadian poet, essayist and scholar Anne Carson was sweeping the floorboards of her home in Reykjavik, Iceland, and ignoring the calls blowing up her phone.
Lauded for what the jury described as a “bold and inventive oeuvre” that “has created new forms for contemporary literature,” Carson sounded surprised, but very happy when she eventually gave the Nobel Prize Committee a call back, said Ingrid Carlberg, the Swedish Academy’s permanent secretary at the Nobel press conference.
Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson’s life was marked indelibly when she began to study ancient Greek in high school. Carson is an academic at heart, and the classical tradition has shaped her work as a teacher, translator and writer. With her first book Eros the Bittersweet (1986), she founded her own classical tradition, unearthing ancient stories and characters and painting them with her inventive, genre-bending brush.
Her “often-unexpected literary constellations” at once tie Carson to and free her from the bounds of classical stories, according to the chair of the Nobel Committee for Literature Anders Olsson. In her lyrical poem “The Glass Essay,” Carson interweaves the narrative of a woman visiting her mother in northern Canada with the words of Emily Brontë, whose books the woman is reading. The result is a meditation on loneliness, grief and poetry shepherded along by these three solitary women.
“Most people read the Autobiography of Red, it seems to be accessible,” said Carson in an interview following the prize announcement. The 1998 novel in verse plucks the characters of Herakles and Geryon out of ancient legend – Herakles the hero, Geryon the three-bodied giant from whom he steals cattle and slays – to place them down on a modern-day island in the Atlantic, then in Buenos Aires, then Peru. The two fall in love, are torn asunder, come back together and so on. Autobiography of Red drew strong and positive reactions at the time of its publishing; the Nation critic Bruce Hainley described the poem as “a brilliant book about desire, the ancient Greek poet Steischoros, volcanoes and the joyful brutalities of seeing and blindness,” and Carson herself as a “philosopher of heartbreak.”
Despite her devotion to ancient stories, Carson is a deeply modern author, said Steve Sem-Sandberg, a writer and member of the Swedish Academy. “She connects our contemporary mores, ways of living, always through the antiquity,” he said at the ceremony. “The mixture between those two gives an enormous energy to her writing. Nobody writes like her, and nobody would even, I think, dare to do this in this way.”
Over her four decades of creation, Carson has played within and ventured beyond the bounds of the literary form. She has collaborated with visual artists and choreographers, directors of opera and theater. Since the 1990s, her work has had “outstanding importance” for the international art and literary scenes, Olsson said.
Her most recent book of poetry Wrong Norma and her essay “The Gender of Sound” were published in 2024 and 2025 respectively. Carson spends her time between Iceland and Ann Arbor, Michigan, with her husband and collaborator Robert Currie.
“Carson once described boredom as her arch enemy,” Olsson said. It’s a foe that she battles “with drastic humor and wit.”

sources.news_title: Toronto author Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature
sources.text:
What to know
- Toronto-born poet and author Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature.
- Carson is the second Canadian woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, after Alice Munro won in 2013.
- The Swedish Academy praised Carson for her “bold and inventive oeuvre” and her playful dialogue with the classical tradition.
- Carson studied Greek poetry at the University of Toronto, earning a bachelor’s degree, master’s degree and PhD.
- She has published more than 25 books, essays, poetry collections and translations, including Autobiography of Red and Wrong Norma.
Toronto-born poet and University of Toronto alumna Anne Carson has won a Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the second Canadian woman to receive the award.
The 2026 Nobel Prize was announced earlier on Thursday, and awarded the Canadian author “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
Carson is the second Canadian woman to have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, after short story author Alice Munro received the award in 2013.
Who is Anne Carson?
Carson was born in Toronto in 1950, and enrolled at the University of Toronto to study Greek poetry in 1968, earning a bachelor’s degree in 1974, a master’s in 1975, and a PhD in 1981. She went on to teach at various universities, including McGill University, Michigan University, and Princeton University. Throughout her career, the author has combined poetry writing and translation work.
The Canadian author’s first book is Eros the Bittersweet: An Essay, published in 1986 by Princeton University Press. The essay grew out of her doctoral thesis Odi et Amo Ergo Sum, which was published in 1981, a classical study literary work led by Eros, the ancient Greek god of love. This book created the foundation for her next works.
Throughout her career, Carson published over 25 major books, essays, poetry collections and translations, including Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse in 1998, which is considered one of her greatest works, said to demonstrate her ability to actualize classical literature, according to the Swedish Academy.
The novel’s sequel, Red Doc>, has led her to become the first two-time winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize in 2014, after she won the first award in 2001 for the prose collection Men in the Off Hours. She was also the first woman to win Britain’s T.S. Eliot Prize in 2001 for The Beauty of the Husband.
Her most recent major works include a collection of prose and poetry with her own drawn illustrations titled Wrong Norma, published in 2024, and The Gender of Sound, an essay published in 2025 that examines how Western culture associates specific sounds with gender and power.
‘What a day for Canadian literature’: reaction kicks in
Reactions to the 2026 Nobel Prize announcement are starting to kick in online, with many sharing their love for the Canadian author on social media.
“What a day for Canadian literature and for classicists! So happy to wake up to this! Congratulations, Anne Carson!” one person wrote on Instagram.
“So deserved! For years, she’s been my prediction and now: at last!” another user said.
“These books have walked me through this life. Thank you Anne Carson!” a different person said.
“Our true Canadian legend! Congratulations!” another user added.

sources.news_title: Canadian author Anne Carson awarded 2026 Literature Nobel
sources.text:
Canadian author Anne Carson has been awarded the prestigious 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for her groundbreaking and inventive body of work that masterfully bridges classical traditions with contemporary literary forms, inspiring new possibilities in writing.
Key Points
- Canadian author Anne Carson was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday for her 'bold and inventive oeuvre' that creatively engages with classical traditions.
- Carson's distinctive work spans poetry, translation, and literary scholarship, uniquely blending classical Greek literature with contemporary writing forms.
- Her career is defined by exploring the relationship between language, classical texts, and creating new literary forms, often placing ancient authors alongside modern writers.
- Notable works like Autobiography of Red (published in 1998) reshape classical material, transforming mythological figures into contemporary narratives.
- Carson's experimentation extends to unconventional forms, such as Nox (published in 2010) as a memorial, and collaborations with various artists, demonstrating her freedom with literary conventions.
The Nobel Foundation on Thursday awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature to Canadian author Anne Carson 'for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature'.
The Swedish Academy, which announced the prize, recognised Carson's distinctive body of work spanning poetry, translation and literary scholarship, highlighting the way she has brought together classical Greek literature and contemporary forms of writing.
Carson's Unique Literary Approach
Born on June 21, 1950, in Toronto, Carson has throughout her career moved between poetry, translation and teaching, with much of her work exploring the relationship between language, classical texts and the creation of new literary forms.
According to the Nobel Prize organisation, Carson's writing is rooted in the intersection between 'the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning'.
The author has also identified the etymology of words as a starting point for her work.
Her engagement with classical literature has been a defining feature of her career.
Her translations from Classical Greek include Sappho's fragments in If Not, Winter (2002), as well as Sophocles' Electra (2001) and Antigone (2015) and Euripides' Bakkhai (2015).
The Nobel Prize citation particularly reflects Carson's ability to bring together seemingly distant literary voices and traditions.
Her work frequently places classical authors alongside modern writers, creating what the Nobel committee describes as unexpected literary constellations.
Engaging With Classical Traditions
One early landmark was Eros the Bittersweet, published in 1986.
In the long essay, Carson examines Eros through the poetry of Sappho and explores the tension between lovers as a source of poetic energy.
Carson describes this approach as a 'stereoscopic vision' that allows me to 'hold in equipoise two perspectives at once'.
That method can also be seen in Economy of the Unlost (1999), where the 6th-century BC Greek poet Simonides of Keos is placed alongside Paul Celan, and in Men in the Off Hours (2000), which brings the historian Thucydides into conversation with Virginia Woolf.
The Nobel Prize organisation said it was through such 'often unexpected, literary constellations' that Carson moved away from lyrical poetry centred on a single narrative self and helped inspire new forms of contemporary literature.
Carson's ability to reshape classical material is perhaps most evident in Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, published in 1998.
The work takes inspiration from fragments by the sixth-century BC Greek poet Stesichoros concerning Geryon, the winged red monster encountered in the myth of Heracles.
Carson transforms the mythological figure into a vulnerable young protagonist and recasts the ancient story as a contemporary coming-of-age narrative.
Transforming Ancient Narratives
The book combines poetry, mythology and fiction while exploring love, violence, vulnerability and loss.
In doing so, it illustrates the approach for which Carson has become known: using ancient literature not simply as material to translate or preserve, but as a foundation for creating something new.
Her 1995 collection Glass, Irony, and God similarly demonstrated her interest in crossing conventional literary boundaries.
Its celebrated long poem The Glass Essay blends poetry, narrative, literary criticism and reflections on abandonment, weaving Emily Brontë's world into the story of a woman confronting grief and an ended relationship.
Carson has also approached intimate subjects through unconventional literary forms.
The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos (2001) explores a fractured marriage through a mixture of prose and verse, with each of its 29 sections opening with lines from the Romantic poet John Keats.
Among Carson's most distinctive works is Nox, published in 2010 as a memorial to her brother Michael, who died in Denmark in 2000.
Rather than taking the conventional form of a book, Nox is constructed as a box containing an accordion-folded sequence of photographs, letters and texts.
The work incorporates Carson's translation of Catullus' famous elegy for his own deceased brother, creating a connection between ancient mourning and Carson's personal loss.
Innovative Forms And Collaborations
The Nobel Prize organisation described the work as 'a creation as sculptural as it is literary'.
Carson's experimentation has continued into her later work.
Float (2016) consists of 22 chapbooks that can be read in different orders, while Wrong Norma, published in 2024, brings together a diverse collection of texts with a strong performative element.
Her work has also extended beyond conventional literary forms through collaborations with visual artists, choreographers, opera productions and theatre directors.
The Nobel Prize organisation said Carson's willingness to cross 'various artistic and academic fields' demonstrates the freedom with which she approaches established literary conventions.
Throughout her career, Carson has combined scholarship and creative writing, using classical texts, linguistic investigation and contemporary experience to challenge the boundaries between poetry, fiction, essay and translation.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, according to the Swedish Academy's citation, recognises precisely that ability to transform inherited literary traditions into new forms.
The prize motivation states that Carson has produced 'bold and inventive' work that remains in 'playful dialogue with the classical tradition' while creating new possibilities for contemporary literature.

sources.news_title: Canadian Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
sources.text:
Canadian Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
The Swedish Academy praised the 76-year-old poet and essayist’s work for being ‘bold and inventive’.
Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, the award-giving body has announced.
Carson was selected “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy said in a statement on Thursday.
The 76-year-old, whose work is praised for blurring the lines of poetry and fiction, and for giving ancient works new translation, is also a professor of classics.
She has written more than 20 books, some of which have been adapted into plays, and has received numerous literary awards.
“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” the academy said.
“She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work. Her translations from Classical Greek may be regarded as independent works in their own right.”
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the academy, which awards the prize worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m), said Carson “was very taken by surprise”.
“We didn’t have so much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind.”
Shortly after the announcement, Carson reacted to her win to Icelandic broadcaster RUV. “Crazy. I think they’re all crazy … Well, you know, it’s crazy,” she said.
Carson, who was born in Toronto, also spends time in Iceland, where she also has citizenship.
One of her most notable works includes the Beauty of the Husband, a poignant and moving book-length narrative poem depicting a doomed marriage.
The Trojan Women, published in 2021, is a graphic retelling of Euripides’s ancient story, infused with modern vernacular.
In August 2024, she revealed in the London Review of Books that she was living with Parkinson’s disease.
The Nobel Prize, awarded by the Swedish Academy, is widely considered the most prestigious international award in literature.
Last year’s prize was won by Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai.
Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in literature, science and peace have been awarded since 1901.
Literature was the fourth of this year’s Nobels to be announced this week, following medicine, physics and chemistry. The peace winner will be announced in Oslo on Friday.

sources.news_title: Nobel Prize in Literature goes to Canadian poet and essayist
sources.text:
Anne Carson, the Toronto-born poet and scholar who’s said to have invented her own genre with work that blends the ancient and the avant-garde, has won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
The famously private Carson became the 123rd Nobel laureate in literature on Thursday, thrusting her somewhat reluctantly into the limelight, according to Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary to the Swedish Academy.
“We didn’t have much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland where she’s listening to the wind,” Carlberg said.
“She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”
Carlberg said the academy rewarded Carson for her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney commended Carson on social media, calling her win “a proud moment for Canada.”
“With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics. She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” Carney wrote on X.
A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson is renowned as a master of esoterica. She’s defied literary conventions with a bibliography of more than 20 books of poetry, essays, plays, libretti and translations of ancient Greek texts.
“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel committee for literature.
She’s amassed a devoted readership and a raft of critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.
Elizabeth Harvey, a retired English professor at the University of Toronto, described how Carson manages to “invent and reinvent form.”
“She takes things that don’t look like poetry, like a lecture or an essay, and makes it into poetry,” she said, pointing to Carson’s lyric essays.
“They look like prose pieces, but they’re really deeply poetic in their sensibility.”
But as Carson’s profile has grown over four decades, the particulars of her personal life have remained elusive.
Her public reticence is encapsulated by her scant book-jacket biography: “Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek mythology.”
Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and various accounts suggest she studied classics at the University of Toronto, and has held teaching positions at institutions including McGill University, Michigan University and Princeton University.
The Swedish Academy confirmed her year and city of birth, but offered few other details.
Concetta Principe, an assistant professor of English at Trent University who wrote a book on Carson, recalled first reading the writer’s author bio.
“It was like two sentences. That’s unusual,” she said. “In that way, it signified humility -- that’s how I saw it initially, and I do still feel that to be the case with her.”
But Principe said she also sees it as a statement about the role of the author.
“We associate what’s on the page with the writer. We think it’s the writer’s life story that we’re reading, and that brings us close to the writer,” she said.
“I think her resistance to sharing is a way of reminding us that even if we think we have found her, even if we had all her biography, we still wouldn’t grasp where she is in the text, (or) what of her life is really there.”
After Carson’s PhD thesis in 1981, she made her publishing debut in 1986 with academic essays on love, “Eros the Bittersweet.”
That book was formative for Louis Ruprecht, director of the Hellenic Studies Institute at Georgia State University.
He said he picked it up when he was a newly minted PhD studying Sappho.
“I was mesmerized and blown away by the book. And when I got back to Atlanta, I wrote her a fan letter,” Ruprecht recalled.
She responded, and they corresponded for a while, he said. They talked mostly about the work -- “we had Sappho in common,” he said.
Carson gained recognition with a series of genre-bending books in the 1990s establishing her style of culling from the literary canon to explore eternal themes. She invoked influences ranging from the Bronte sisters to the Greek poet Stesichorus in the early sixth century BC.
Carson cemented her reputation with her 1998 novel in verse, “Autobiography of Red,” which reimagines the 10th labour of Hercules, telling the life story of the monster he slays, Geryon.
Carson became the inaugural Canadian winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize for “Man in the Off Hours” in 2001, and was awarded England’s T.S. Eliot Prize for “The Beauty of the Husband” the same year.
In 2014, Carson took the Griffin again for “Red Doc,” a quasi-sequel to “Autobiography of Red.” It made her the first two-time winner of the prize.
At the time, she told The Canadian Press she was surprised to win, partly because she doesn’t “really like the book” and partly because she’d already won the honour and “thought it wouldn’t be fair” to get it again.
“I don’t mean it’s a bad book,” she said. “I mean, I don’t know if it’s a good book or a bad book. I just have a vision when I start of what a thing is and sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t.”
Scott Griffin, the award’s benefactor, said Thursday that Carson’s win is a win for Canada and Canadian poetry.
“Anne Carson has raised the profile of poetry to its rightful place, in my opinion, right to the pinnacle of literature,” he said.
Griffin got to know Carson a little bit when they travelled to Edinburgh together after she won the inaugural prize.
“On stage, she tends to come through -- sometimes, for some people -- as a little bit severe,” he said. “But she’s very warm and loves to have fun.”
Carson also prevailed in the poetry category at the 2020 Governor General’s Literary Awards for “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which in trademark style blends the story of Helen of Troy with elements from Marilyn Monroe’s life. She was shortlisted again two years later for “H of H Playbook,” a retelling of Euripides’s Greek tragedy, Herakles.
Among her more recent books is 2024’s “Wrong Norma,” her first original work since 2016. The collection of “poetic prose pieces” was published alongside her own illustrations.
Carson is the second Canadian woman to be named a Nobel laureate in the literature category, following short story master Alice Munro’s 2013 win.
The American playwright and novelist Saul Bellow, who was born in Montreal and grew up in Chicago, was awarded the Nobel in 1976.
The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or roughly $1.7 million.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.
Nicole Thompson, The Canadian Press

sources.news_title: Canadian Poet Anne Carson Wins 2026 Nobel in Literature
sources.text:
The Swedish Academy awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday to Anne Carson, the Canadian poet, essayist and classicist whose work has spent four decades folding Greek myth, philology and private grief into forms that resist every label the academy might have reached for — "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature."
Ingrid Carlberg, the academy's permanent secretary, read the citation at 1 p.m. in Stockholm. Carson, 76, is the first poet to receive the prize since Louise Glück in 2020 and the first Canadian since Alice Munro in 2013 — and, after years near the top of bookmakers' lists, one of the least surprising choices the academy has made in a decade that included a Tanzanian-born novelist, a French memoirist and a Hungarian apocalyptic. The prize carries an award of 12 million Swedish kronor, about $1.2 million.
"Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning," said Anders Olsson, chairman of the Nobel Committee for Literature. The academy's own summary of her career noted that she has combined poetry with translation and university teaching throughout it, a description that undersells how thoroughly the three activities run together in her books.
The work most readers will reach for first is "Autobiography of Red" (1998), a novel in verse that takes the red-winged monster Geryon — slain by Heracles in the fragments of the Greek poet Stesichorus — and recasts him, in the committee's words, as a "tender 'hero' devoted to his mother" who, after sexual abuse by his brother, "falls in love with the smug and boorish Heracles." The book made Carson a crossover figure: a classicist with a cult readership and a poet whose line breaks could carry a coming-of-age story. "The Beauty of the Husband" (2001), subtitled "a fictional essay in 29 tangos," made her the first woman to win Britain's T.S. Eliot Prize. "Nox" (2010), an accordion-folded facsimile of the scrapbook she assembled after her estranged brother's death, built around her translation of a Catullus elegy, is the book that most directly shows the method: a dead language used to approach a death.
Her translations are a body of work in themselves. "If Not, Winter" (2002) rendered the fragments of Sappho with the gaps left visible as brackets on the page, an approach that has shaped how a generation of readers encounters the poet. She has translated Euripides, Sophocles and Aeschylus for the stage, often with deliberately contemporary idiom, and her first book, "Eros the Bittersweet" (1986), was a work of scholarship on desire in Greek lyric that doubled as a statement of her own aesthetics.
Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and has taught classics and comparative literature at McGill, the University of Michigan, New York University and elsewhere. She received a MacArthur fellowship in 2000 and Spain's Princess of Asturias Award for Letters in 2020. She is famously reluctant with biography — her books carry the author note that she "was born in Canada and teaches ancient Greek for a living" — and had not commented publicly on the prize by Thursday evening.
The choice continues a pattern the academy has followed since its 2018 scandal and reorganization: laureates with substantial bodies of work and long critical standing, rather than the provocations of the Bob Dylan year, and an alternation across continents and forms. The last three prizes went to a Norwegian playwright, a South Korean novelist and the Hungarian László Krasznahorkai, honored in 2025 "for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art." Carson's citation, with its "playful dialogue," reads almost as a deliberate change of key.
The literature prize has now been awarded 119 times to 123 laureates since 1901. Carson is the 18th woman among them.
The Nobel week concludes Friday with the Peace Prize, announced at 11 a.m. in Oslo from a field of 287 nominees, and Monday with the economics prize in Stockholm. The laureates receive their medals on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death.

sources.news_title: Genre-defying Canadian poet Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
Canadian writer Anne Carson wins Nobel literature prize
sources.text:
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in literature for playful, genre-blending works that fuse the classical and the modern.
Toronto-born Carson, 76, draws on themes and stories from ancient Greek and Roman literature for works that often blend elements of poetry, essay and fiction.
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said the author was in Iceland "listening to the wind" when the academy reached her to notify her of the win.
"She was very taken by surprise," Carlberg said on Thursday.
Carson's books include Eros the Bittersweet, a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, verse novel Autobiography of Red, Men in the Off Hours, a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada's Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001 and Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.
She also has translated works of classical Greek literature that, the Swedish Academy said, "may be regarded as independent works in their own right".
They include If Not, Winter, based on poem fragments by Sappho, Sophocles' tragic plays Electra and Antigone and Euripides' Bakkhai.
"Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning," said Anders Olsson, chair of the literature committee.
Olsson said Carson's juxtaposition of influences ranging from the ancient Greeks to John Keats, Virginia Woolf and Emily Bronte "leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and art forms".
Carson has taught classics at several North American universities and has lived in Iceland, where she and her husband, Robert Currie, were granted citizenship in 2022.
She also has drawn on her own life for works such as Nox, which was published in 2010 and dealt with the decades-long absence and then death of her brother Michael.
Olsson called it "a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother".
It also includes Carson's translation of an elegy by the Roman poet Catullus for his own brother.
Among her most recent work is, Wrong Norma, a 2024 a wide-ranging collection of pieces from publications including The Paris Review and The New Yorker, accompanied by Carson's hand-drawn illustrations.
Also that year, Carson wrote in the London Review of Books about being diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.
She said "a symptom particularly mortifying to me was that my handwriting disintegrated. Hard to describe or explain the shame of bad handwriting."
The prize was announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm.
Three science awards were announced earlier this week.
The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
The physics award recognised a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.
The chemistry prize recognised two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
This week ends with Friday's peace prize.
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.
The prize money is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $A1.7 million) per prize.

sources.news_title: Anne Carson Wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for Genre-Defying Body of Work
sources.text:
Rabat – Canadian poet, essayist, classicist, and translator Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, with the Swedish Academy recognizing a body of work that has persistently challenged the boundaries between literary genres and brought the ancient world into conversation with contemporary life.
The Academy selected the 76-year-old writer for her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
Carson has built an unusually difficult body of work to categorize. Her books move between poetry, prose, literary criticism, translation, drama, and scholarship, often making the distinctions between these forms deliberately unstable.
Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson developed an interest in classical literature while still at school, after a Latin teacher began teaching her ancient Greek during lunch breaks. She went on to study classics at the University of Toronto, eventually earning a PhD in the field, and later taught classical languages and literature at universities in Canada and the United States.
That classical training became one of the defining features of her literary career.
Bringing ancient myths into modern literature
Carson’s first major book, “Eros the Bittersweet”, published in 1986, examined desire through ancient Greek literature and established a method that would characterize much of her later work: rigorous scholarship presented through an unusually literary and associative form.
Her best-known work, “Autobiography of Red”, published in 1998, further demonstrated that approach. Described as a novel in verse, the book reimagines the ancient Greek myth of Geryon, a red-winged monster associated with one of Herakles’ labors, as the story of a sensitive adolescent navigating love, heartbreak, and identity.
Rather than treating classical mythology as a fixed inheritance, Carson transformed it into a framework for examining modern emotional life. The result blurred the line between an ancient myth, a contemporary coming-of-age story, and a work of experimental poetry.
That refusal to remain within established literary categories has remained a hallmark of Carson’s work.
Her books have included “Men in the Off Hours”, which combines poems with prose, verse essays, epitaphs, and other forms; “The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos”, which explores marital breakdown and desire; “Decreation”, which moves between poetry, criticism, philosophy, and dramatic forms; and “Nox”, an experimental book-length work centered on the death of her brother.
Carson’s work has consequently resisted easy placement within the traditional literary canon. Rather than choosing between poetry and criticism, or between the ancient and modern worlds, she has repeatedly treated those categories as material that can be rearranged.
Reimagining the classics through translation
Her contribution to contemporary literature also extends to translation.
Carson has translated works by ancient Greek writers including Sappho, Euripides, Sophocles, and Aeschylus. Her 2002 “If Not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho” is particularly notable for preserving the gaps and missing passages in Sappho’s surviving poetry rather than attempting to conceal what has been lost over centuries.
Her translations have similarly questioned what it means to carry a work from one language and historical period into another. Carson has described translation as occupying a space between two languages, where multiple possible meanings can exist simultaneously rather than producing one definitive equivalent.
This relationship with incompleteness, ambiguity, and fragments is particularly significant to her broader literary project. Carson frequently treats gaps in language, history, memory, and narrative not as obstacles to be overcome but as spaces in which new forms of writing can emerge.
Her approach has earned her a reputation as one of the most distinctive figures in contemporary poetry. She has received numerous major literary honors, including the Griffin Poetry Prize, the T.S. Eliot Prize, a Guggenheim Fellowship, and a MacArthur Fellowship. Her 2024 collection “Wrong Norma” was a finalist for the National Book Award and won the National Book Critics Circle Award.
For Carson, however, the boundaries between scholarship and creative writing have never been merely formal questions. Her work has helped broaden the possibilities of what contemporary poetry can contain: classical philology, fragments of ancient texts, photographs, essays, philosophical inquiry, autobiography, mythology, and forms borrowed from music and theater.
That has also allowed her to make the classical canon feel less like a closed archive and more like a living body of material that can be questioned, translated, distorted, and rewritten.
Carson’s significance extends beyond her individual books. Her work has contributed to a wider rethinking of the literary canon by demonstrating that ancient texts can be neither museum pieces nor objects of purely academic study. They can instead become raw material for contemporary writers seeking new ways to approach subjects that remain remarkably persistent across centuries.
The Nobel Prize in Literature is awarded for an author’s overall body of work rather than a single book. Carson will receive the Nobel medal and diploma and a prize of 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately $1.2 million, at the Nobel ceremony in Stockholm in December.
According to Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, she informed Carson of the decision by telephone shortly before the public announcement.
Carson was in Iceland at the time, Carlberg said, where she was listening to the wind.
The Nobel announcement now adds one of literature’s highest distinctions to a career that has spent decades questioning what literature itself can be.

The 76-year-old writer is known for her hybrid style, combining poetry and prose, as well as contemporary stories with ancient myth.
The Academy stated: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work.”
Among Carson’s best-known works are her 1986 debut "Eros the Bittersweet", a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature; her 1998 work, often heralded as her greatest, "Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse", a queer coming-of-age story that reworks a Greek poem about Heracles; "The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos" (2001); and "Norma Jeane Baker of Troy" (2019), which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.
Her most recent work is "Wrong Norma", which was published in 2024.
By winning the Nobel Prize, Carson becomes only the 19th woman to win the Nobel Prize for Literature, with recent winners including Han Kang in 2024, Annie Ernaux in 2022 and Louis Glück in 2020.
As of today, the literature prize has been awarded by the Nobel committee of the Swedish Academy 119 times to a total of 123 winners (four literature prizes have been shared between multiple laureates).
Last year's prize was won by postmodern Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art.” Susan Sontag previously described the author as “the contemporary Hungarian master of apocalypse.”
The literature prize is the fourth to be announced this week, following the 2026 Nobels in medecine, physics and chemistry.
Each prize this year comes with 12 million Swedish kronor (€1.07 million). The winners also receive an 18-carat gold medal and a diploma.
The winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced on Friday and the final prize, the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, is to be announced on Monday.
Nobel Prize award ceremonies are held on 10 December, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death in 1896.
